what: 3:1 gear-driven rack trolley and passive rigid pendulum: finite command shaping. One motor moves a guided rack trolley through a 36T/12T gear pair with a 3:1 speed increase. A rigid hanging arm pivots freely on the trolley and has no motor of its own. Its two connected beams have a 216 mm span between the outer holes; the mass is distributed along them. Moving the support can set this passive load swinging, and stopping the trolley does not instantly stop the load. SwayShift compares two programs on exactly the same saved machine. Both use the same absolute waypoints: nominally 22 mm from the saved datum, then 44 mm, giving two nominally equal 22 mm moves in the same direction. The main program starts the second move half a measured swing period after the first starts; the in-phase comparison waits a full period between starts. The total requested travel and the final requested trolley position are the same. Both programs calculate each relative motor command from a fresh encoder reading; their actual command arguments and motion histories can therefore differ slightly. Watch the load after the transfer, as well as the trolley during it. A separate native free-swing calibration measured T = 0.7571 s. The programs request start gaps of 0.380 s and 0.760 s; the native observer measures the actual starts. One motor drives a rack trolley through a 3:1 speed increase. A freely hinged rigid pendulum has a 216 mm hole span. Compare the same nominal 22 mm + 22 mm transfer with half-period or full-period timing between move starts, then observe the passive load after arrival.
try: Reset the complete scene, load this model’s example program and run it. Reset again before every repeat or comparison.
Identify the driven trolley and the freely hinged arm. Before running, predict whether the load can continue moving after motor A has reached its final position.

Follow the two trolley moves and the intervening pause. The relevant interval runs from the start of the first move to the start of the second, not from the end of the first move. Both moves take a finite time.

Observe the passive angle while the trolley holds the outer 44 mm waypoint, during stage 3 and before the later slow return. Compare the full swing envelope over the observation interval: a single moment when the arm crosses vertical can hide a large angular velocity.

Import the entire same swayshift.ldr model afresh, then run programs/swayshift-in-phase.bw. This comparison uses a full swing period between move starts. The machine, absolute waypoints, requested speeds and fresh-encoder command algorithm stay the same.

Compare both runs in the same clock window, from the first move start plus 2*T to that start plus 6*T. Also compare each run from its actual second-move completion plus T through completion plus 5*T. The half-period program finishes earlier, so it has more passive settling time in the common-clock window; the arrival-relative comparison gives equal time since arrival.

Reload the complete saved model before every repeat or program change. Resetting the motor encoder does not reset the hanging arm’s angle or velocity, and returning the trolley alone does not recreate the original scene.
why: A moving suspension point applies a disturbance to the passive pendulum. For small swings, two similar trolley moves produce two similar oscillatory responses. If the second response begins half a period after the first, their phases oppose and the remaining swing can be reduced. With a full-period separation, their phases align and the remaining swing can be larger. This is command shaping: timing the drive motion uses the load’s natural rhythm without directly driving its angle. The ideal cancellation law assumes a dominant linear swing mode and matching actual support motions. Friction, damping, finite swing angle, timing error and motor tracking can leave a residual even at the intended half-period spacing.
matters: A transported load can reach its destination while still moving relative to its support. Comparing actual trolley position and passive swing separates arrival from settling. The same timing idea is useful in crane motion and flexible positioning systems. This complete 204-part model and both finite programs passed the independently frozen native qualification on the identified Brickwright runtime. It remains an experimental add-on: browser execution, manual control and a physical build are UNTESTED. The native result is scoped to the recorded model and runtime.
question: With the same nominal 22 mm + 22 mm waypoints and command algorithm, only the start-to-start interval changes from about half a swing period to about one full period. Should the final requested trolley position change, and which timing should leave more swing?
answer: The final requested trolley position stays the same because the two absolute waypoints are unchanged. In the small-angle reference, half-period spacing makes the two oscillatory responses oppose; full-period spacing makes them add. The accepted native pair measured 0.265 degrees RMS residual angle with half-period timing versus 10.465 degrees with full-period timing in the common window, about 97.47 percent lower. At equal time after each actual arrival, the values were 0.266 and 10.355 degrees, about 97.43 percent lower. These are measured native results, not a promise of zero sway or a hardware result. Actual command arguments and trolley histories can differ slightly despite using the same waypoint algorithm.
further: T is the measured free-swing period of the complete prepared pendulum while its support is held. Here T = 0.7570673941 s; the requested start gaps are 0.380 s and 0.760 s. For a physical pendulum the small-angle reference is T = 2*pi*sqrt(I_p/(m*g*d)), using actual pivot inertia I_p and pivot-to-center-of-mass distance d. The 216 mm hole span alone is insufficient.

For two identical finite moves in a linear undamped model, the residual responses combine with magnitude 2*A1*abs(cos(pi*delta/T)), where A1 is the residual amplitude from one move and delta is their start separation. Delta = T/2 predicts opposition; delta = T predicts addition. This is a response prediction, not a prescribed load trajectory.

The comparison uses finite commands. Only the executable start_gap line changes between the two programs. Each move targets an unchanged absolute waypoint and subtracts a fresh encoder reading to obtain the relative motor argument. Thus the nominal half-distances and algorithm match, while actual relative command arguments and trolley histories can differ slightly. The independent observer measures those differences.

Both preregistered observation windows passed. The half-period transfer arrived 0.385 s earlier, giving it extra decay time in the common-clock window. Measured control ringdown gives an amplitude multiplier of about 0.9895 per half-period, roughly a 1 percent decrease. The large reduction also survived the matched arrival-relative window from actual second completion plus T through plus 5*T. It therefore does not depend only on the earlier finish.

Predict what would happen if the hanging arm became longer or its ballast moved. Its period could change, so the same timing could lose its advantage. A two-command shaper is sensitive to period error; it is not a universal cure for vibration or external disturbances.

Compare Rack Shuttle for the drive conversion, Sky Courier for a suspended load whose sway is separate from encoder arrival, and Resonance Lab for the effect of drive rhythm on a passive oscillator. SwayShift changes the timing of a completed transfer while keeping the mechanism fixed.

The numerical results refer to the identified native runtime. It applies its normal gear-body mass/inertia conditioning and motor-rotor inertia; the 32.2 g trolley and 10.1 g passive pendulum are unadjusted. SwayShift adds no mass or inertia override. These native results are not a measured hardware response; details are in SOURCES.md.
formula: Small-angle physical pendulum: T approximately 2*pi*sqrt(I_p/(m*g*d)). Two identical finite move responses in the linear undamped reference: A_pair = 2*A1*abs(cos(pi*delta/T)); delta is the start-to-start separation. Half-period timing delta = T/2 opposes the responses; full-period timing delta = T aligns them. Actual damping, finite angles and controller tracking must be measured; zero residual is not guaranteed.
